claim: The retinal neuroepithelium (RNE) is the organ precursor that later gives rise to all neurons of the mature retina.
source: Here, the retinal neuroepithelium (RNE) is the organ precursor that later gives rise to all neurons of the mature retina (Fuhrmann, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fuhrmann, 2010.

claim: The hemispheric RNE that is located in the optic cup develops from the epithelial optic vesicles.
source: The hemispheric RNE that is located in the optic cup develops from the epithelial optic vesicles (Bazin-Lopez et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bazin-Lopez et al., 2015.

claim: RNE formation involves complex epithelial rearrangements including tissue elongation, sheet invagination and epithelial sheet movements.
source: Its formation involves complex epithelial rearrangements including tissue elongation, sheet invagination and epithelial sheet movements (Martinez-Morales et al., 2009; Heermann et al., 2015; Kwan et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Martinez-Morales et al., 2009; Heermann et al., 2015; Kwan et al., 2012.

claim: In mouse and human retinal organoid in vitro cultures, the optic vesicle epithelium self-organizes into a hemispherical shape due to high proliferation in a confined space.
source: It has been shown in mouse and human retinal organoid in vitro cultures that the optic vesicle epithelium self-organizes into a hemispherical shape due to high proliferation in a confined space (Eiraku et al., 2011; Nakano et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eiraku et al., 2011; Nakano et al., 2012.

claim: In zebrafish and Xenopus, RNE development continues even when cell proliferation is blocked.
source: However, work in zebrafish and Xenopus shows that RNE development continues even when cell proliferation is blocked (Harris and Hartenstein, 1991; Kwan et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harris and Hartenstein, 1991; Kwan et al., 2012.

claim: In teleosts, RNE morphogenesis occurs by rearrangements of a continuous epithelium, the bilayered optic vesicle.
source: In teleosts, RNE morphogenesis occurs by rearrangements of a continuous epithelium, the bilayered optic vesicle (Schmitt and Dowling, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schmitt and Dowling, 1994.

claim: The distal layer of the optic vesicle develops into the RNE and part of the proximal layer develops into retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).
source: The distal layer of the optic vesicle develops into the RNE and part of the proximal layer develops into retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).
evidence: This is a statement of established developmental biology knowledge about optic vesicle differentiation.

claim: Basal constriction of RNE cells is important for RNE invagination.
source: Work in zebrafish and medaka showed that basal constriction of RNE cells is important for RNE invagination (brown cell, Figure 1A) (Martinez-Morales et al., 2009; Bogdanović et al., 2012; Nicolás-Pérez et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Martinez-Morales et al., 2009; Bogdanović et al., 2012; Nicolás-Pérez et al., 2016.

claim: A subpopulation of prospective RNE cells is located in the proximal epithelial layer at the onset of optic cup morphogenesis.
source: However, given that a subpopulation of prospective RNE cells is located in the proximal epithelial layer, at the onset of optic cup morphogenesis (OCM), it is not clear whether basal constrictions alone can drive RNE formation or whether these cells play an additional role.
evidence: This is stated as an established observation that motivates the research question.

claim: Proximal prospective RNE cells move into the distal, invaginating neuroepithelium by a process called rim involution.
source: The proximal prospective RNE cells move into the distal, invaginating neuroepithelium by a process called rim involution (blue cell, Figure 1A) (Kwan et al., 2012; Picker et al., 2009; Heermann et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kwan et al., 2012; Picker et al., 2009; Heermann et al., 2015.

claim: The average basal area of RNE cells was reduced by about 45% during optic cup invagination.
source: Concomitantly, the average basal area of RNE cells was reduced by about 45%.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The reduction in basal area of RNE cells mainly occurred during the first half of the invagination process between 15 ss and 21 ss.
source: This reduction mainly occurred during the first half of the invagination process between 15 ss and 21 ss (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The average apical area of RNE cells increased during invagination.
source: In contrast, the average apical area of cells increased.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At the end of the invagination process, the average apical area was larger than the average basal area of RNE cells.
source: As a result, the average apical area was larger than the average basal area at the end of the process.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RNE cells undergo overall shape changes during invagination and form cones with a narrowing basal surface.
source: This shows that cells undergo overall shape changes during invagination and form cones with a narrowing basal surface (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At the onset of neuroepithelial invagination, the actin marker GFP-UtrophinCH accumulated at the basal side of the RNE.
source: At the onset of neuroepithelial invagination, the actin marker GFP-UtrophinCH (Burkel et al., 2007) accumulated at the basal side of the RNE (Video 1, Figure 1C)
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Video 1 and Figure 1C.

claim: The myosin marker myl12.1-EGFP accumulated at the basal side of the RNE at the onset of neuroepithelial invagination.
source: similarly to the myosin marker, myl12.1-EGFP (Iwasaki et al., 2001) (Video 2, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Video 2 and Figure 1D.

claim: Basal actin and myosin enrichment was specific to the invaginating zone of the neuroepithelium and was not observed in other regions of the optic cup.
source: Basal actin and myosin enrichment was specific to the invaginating zone of the neuroepithelium and was not observed in other regions of the optic cup (Videos 1 and 2, Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Videos 1 and 2, and Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: The basal actomyosin bias spanned about 15% of the RNE height.
source: Quantitative analysis of phalloidin and phosphomyosin intensity distribution along the apicobasal axis of the neuroepithelium showed that the basal actomyosin bias spanned about 15% of the RNE height (Figure 1F,H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis shown in Figures 1F and 1H.

claim: Invagination of the neuroepithelium is accompanied by basal surface area reduction.
source: Thus, we confirmed that invagination of the neuroepithelium is accompanied by basal surface area reduction (Nicolás-Pérez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the data in the manuscript and confirmed by citation to Nicolás-Pérez et al., 2016.

claim: Invaginating RNE cells change their overall shape and feature basal accumulation of contractile actomyosin.
source: We further show that invaginating RNE cells change their overall shape and feature basal accumulation of contractile actomyosin (Figure 1F and H).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 1F and 1H.

claim: Upon 7 h of Rockout treatment, lens structures in treated embryos developed similarly to controls.
source: Upon 7 h of Rockout treatment, lens structures in treated embryos developed similarly to controls (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Upon 7 h of Rockout treatment, the basal actomyosin bias in invaginating RNE cells was markedly reduced.
source: In contrast, the basal actomyosin bias in invaginating RNE cells was markedly reduced (Figure 2A,C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging and quantitative data shown in Figures 2A, 2C, and 2D.

claim: Upon Rockout treatment, the overall staining for phosphomyosin was weaker in the treated embryos.
source: Also, the overall staining for phosphomyosin was weaker in the treated embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 40% of Rockout-treated embryos showed an accumulation of cells at the rim of the cup.
source: 40% of embryos showed an accumulation of cells at the rim of the cup, whereas 30% of embryos showed a milder optic cup phenotype (n = 30 embryos per experiment, N = 5 experiments; 30% of embryos showed stalled development and were thus excluded from the analysis; Figure 2A,B, see Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis of phenotypes across multiple experiments.

claim: 30% of Rockout-treated embryos showed a milder optic cup phenotype.
source: 40% of embryos showed an accumulation of cells at the rim of the cup, whereas 30% of embryos showed a milder optic cup phenotype (n = 30 embryos per experiment, N = 5 experiments; 30% of embryos showed stalled development and were thus excluded from the analysis; Figure 2A,B, see Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis of phenotypes across multiple experiments.

claim: The invagination angle in Rockout treatment was on average 80° compared to 60° in DMSO controls.
source: The invagination angle (defined as the angle between the inner lips of the optic cup and the center of the RNE, see schematic in Figure 2F and Material and methods) was only moderately wider in Rockout treatement with an average of 80° (SEM ± 3.979 n = 15) compared to 60° (SEM ± 2.631 n = 14) in DMSO controls (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: RNE invagination was initiated but appeared delayed in Rockout-treated embryos.
source: Thus, RNE invagination was initiated but was not as efficient in the treated embryos as in controls and appeared delayed (Figure 2A,F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figures 2A and 2F.

claim: RNE invagination still took place in Rockout-treated embryos, albeit with slower kinetics, even when basal actin levels were greatly reduced.
source: This confirmed that RNE invagination still took place, albeit with slower kinetics, even when basal actin levels were greatly reduced (Video 3, Figure 2E,G).
evidence: This is supported by the time-lapse imaging data shown in Video 3 and Figures 2E and 2G.

claim: At 30ss, the basal surface area of the invaginating cells was similar in controls and Rockout-treated embryos.
source: Interestingly, at 30ss, the end point of optic cup invagination, the basal surface area of the invaginating cells was similar in controls and Rockout-treated embryos (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: RNE invagination does not solely depend on basal actomyosin contractility and can be compensated by other mechanisms.
source: This observation suggests that RNE invagination does not solely depend on basal actomyosin contractility and that it can be compensated by other mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that invagination continues despite reduced actomyosin.

claim: RNE formation is accompanied by high proliferation rates.
source: One way to increase cell numbers is proliferation, and it has been shown that RNE formation is accompanied by high proliferation rates (Kwan et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kwan et al., 2012.

claim: Proliferation has been suggested as a driving force for optic cup formation in vitro.
source: In addition, proliferation has been suggested as a driving force for optic cup formation in vitro (Eiraku et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Eiraku et al., 2011.

claim: In zebrafish and Xenopus, optic cup invagination persists even when proliferation is inhibited.
source: In zebrafish and Xenopus, however, optic cup invagination persists even when proliferation is inhibited (Kwan et al., 2012; Harris and Hartenstein, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kwan et al., 2012; Harris and Hartenstein, 1991.

claim: Inhibition of proliferation with hydroxyurea and aphidicolin from 10 ss onwards led to markedly reduced pH3 staining compared to controls.
source: To test whether tissue compaction caused by ongoing proliferation can at all influence RNE invagination, we inhibited proliferation with hydroxyurea and aphidicolin from 10 ss onwards (Kwan et al., 2012), leading to markedly reduced pH3 staining compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Following inhibition of proliferation, the neuroepithelium hosted fewer cells and these cells adopted a more columnar morphology than control cells.
source: Consequently, the neuroepithelium hosted fewer cells and these cells adopted a more columnar morphology than control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D and [Kwan et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D and citation to Kwan et al., 2012.

claim: Following inhibition of proliferation, cells in the RNE displayed a larger average basal area than control cells.
source: Furthermore, following inhibition of proliferation, cells in the RNE displayed a larger average basal area than control cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Optic cup formation still occurred and invagination angles were not severely affected when proliferation was inhibited.
source: Despite this, optic cup formation still occurred and invagination angles were not severely affected (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The total number of cells in the invaginating RNE influences the basal area of single cells.
source: This observation indicated two things a) That the total number of cells in the invaginating RNE influences the basal area of single cells
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cells have larger basal area when there are fewer cells.

claim: RNE invagination can take place even when cells show a broader basal area due to reduced cell proliferation.
source: and b) that RNE invagination can take place even when cells show a broader basal area due to reduced cell proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that invagination continues despite larger basal cell area.

claim: Rim involution is most prominent at the ventral and temporal side of the cup.
source: This phenomenon is most prominent at the ventral and temporal side of the cup and relocates a substantial number of cells from the proximal layer of the optic vesicle into the invaginating RNE (blue cell, Figure 1A) (Kwan et al., 2012; Picker et al., 2009; Heermann et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kwan et al., 2012; Picker et al., 2009; Heermann et al., 2015.

claim: Rim involution relocates a substantial number of cells from the proximal layer of the optic vesicle into the invaginating RNE.
source: This phenomenon is most prominent at the ventral and temporal side of the cup and relocates a substantial number of cells from the proximal layer of the optic vesicle into the invaginating RNE (blue cell, Figure 1A) (Kwan et al., 2012; Picker et al., 2009; Heermann et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kwan et al., 2012; Picker et al., 2009; Heermann et al., 2015.

claim: Rim cells in the Rockout-treated embryos continued to move into the cup.
source: As we noted that rim cells in the Rockout-treated embryos continued to move into the cup (Figure 2E, Video 3), we wondered whether these cell movements could explain the recovery of RNE morphogenesis defects upon Rockout treatment.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 2E and Video 3.

claim: Moving rim cells kept a stable apical domain but were very dynamic at the basal side.
source: Mosaic labeling of rim cells with the membrane marker mKate2-ras and the apical marker Par3-GFP revealed that moving rim cells kept a stable apical domain but were very dynamic at the basal side (Figure 3A, Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3A and Video 4.

claim: Microtubules marked with EMTB-tdTomato did not show significant reorganization during rim involution.
source: As microtubules marked with EMTB-tdTomato did not show significant reorganization during rim involution, we concluded that microtubules were not majorly involved in the cellular dynamics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rim cells extended dynamic lamellipodia-like protrusions in the direction of movement.
source: Instead, we observed that cells extended dynamic lamellipodia-like protrusions in the direction of movement (Figure 3A, Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3A and Video 4.

claim: The lamellipodia-like protrusions of rim cells were actin rich, as shown by GFP-UtrophinCH localization.
source: These protrusions were actin rich, as shown by GFP-UtrophinCH localization (Figure 3B, Video 5), underlining their lamellipodial character.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3B and Video 5.

claim: Lamellipodia were only observed in the rim cells and were not seen in the invaginating RNE cells.
source: Such lamellipodia were only observed in the rim cells and were not seen in the invaginating RNE cells (Figure 3B, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3B and Video 5.

claim: The vast majority of the actin rich protrusions in rim cells occurred in the direction of movement, the leading side of the cells facing the invaginating zone.
source: When we quantified basal protrusive activity during rim migration, we found that the vast majority of the actin rich protrusions occurred in the direction of movement, the leading side of the cells facing the invaginating zone (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: The protrusive activity of rim cells is directional.
source: This showed that the protrusive activity of rim cells is directional.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that protrusions occur predominantly on the leading side.

claim: The directional actin-rich lamellipodia formation and rim migration were still observed in the Rockout condition.
source: Interestingly, the directional actin-rich lamellipodia formation and rim migration were still observed in the Rockout condition (Figure 3F,G, Video 6)
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figures 3F, 3G, and Video 6.

claim: The migratory behavior of rim cells occurs independently of the basal actomyosin bias in the invaginating RNE cells.
source: further indicating that the migratory behavior of rim cells occurs independently of the basal actomyosin bias in the invaginating RNE cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that rim migration continues in Rockout condition.

claim: Rim cells maintained their apicobasal polarity and an apical actin pool associated with the adherens junctions while exhibiting protrusive membrane activity at the basal side.
source: Interestingly, while rim cells exhibited protrusive membrane activity at the basal side, they nevertheless maintained their apicobasal polarity and an apical actin pool associated with the adherens junctions (Figure 3C, Videos 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3C and Videos 7 and 8.

claim: Rim cells are integrated in an intact epithelial sheet and display the migratory behavior as a collective epithelium.
source: This shows that a) rim cells are integrated in an intact epithelial sheet and display the migratory behavior as a collective epithelium
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that rim cells maintain apicobasal polarity and adherens junctions.

claim: Rim cells show characteristics that are intermediate between the epithelial and mesenchymal state.
source: and b) that rim cells show characteristics that are intermediate between the epithelial and mesenchymal state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that rim cells have both epithelial (polarity) and mesenchymal (protrusive) characteristics.

claim: Once rim cells reach the RNE, they change their basal dynamics and establish a stable basal actomyosin pool similar to the basally constricting RNE cells.
source: Once cells reach the RNE, however, they change their basal dynamics and establish a stable basal actomyosin pool similar to the basally constricting RNE cells.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data showing the transition in cell behavior.

claim: Once rim cells reached the RNE and stopped the active migratory behavior, basal actin dynamics changed considerably and mesenchymal characteristics were lost.
source: However, once rim cells reached the RNE, basal actin dynamics changed considerably and mesenchymal characteristics were lost.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data showing the transition in cell behavior.

claim: Lamellipodia formation ceased once rim cells reached the RNE and a pool of stable basal actin was observed similar to the actin distribution in the invaginating RNE cells.
source: Lamellipodia formation ceased and a pool of stable basal actin was observed similar to the actin distribution in the invaginating RNE cells (Figure 3B, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3B and Video 5.

claim: Myosin labeled by DD-myl12b-GFP occurred as dynamic spots at the basal side of cells during rim movement.
source: Likewise, while myosin labeled by DD-myl12b-GFP occurred as dynamic spots at the basal side of cells during rim movement (Video 9, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), it became stably enriched once the cells reached the inner side of the optic cup.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Video 9 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Myosin became stably enriched once rim cells reached the inner side of the optic cup.
source: Likewise, while myosin labeled by DD-myl12b-GFP occurred as dynamic spots at the basal side of cells during rim movement (Video 9, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), it became stably enriched once the cells reached the inner side of the optic cup.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Video 9 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rim cells exhibit dynamic and directional basal lamellipodia formation that coincides with directed migratory behavior.
source: Together, these data show that rim cells exhibit dynamic and directional basal lamellipodia formation that coincides with directed migratory behavior.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the imaging data presented.

claim: Laminin and Chondroitin sulfate were only weakly expressed beneath the developing retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), but showed stronger accumulation in the rim zone, the developing lens placode and the invaginating RNE.
source: Laminin and Chondroitin sulfate were only weakly expressed beneath the developing retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), but showed stronger accumulation in the rim zone, the developing lens placode and the invaginating RNE (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Fibronectin showed preferential staining in the rim zone and the developing lens placode and weaker staining beneath the invaginating RNE.
source: Fibronectin instead showed preferential staining in the rim zone and the developing lens placode and weaker staining beneath the invaginating RNE (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Imaging the focal adhesion markers Integrin-β1-mKate2 and Paxillin-mKate2 revealed dynamic short-lived foci at the basal side of rim cells during time-lapse imaging.
source: Imaging the focal adhesion markers Integrin-β1-mKate2 and Paxillin-mKate2 indeed revealed dynamic short-lived foci at the basal side of rim cells during time-lapse imaging (Videos 10 and 11, Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Videos 10 and 11, and Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Once rim cells reach the RNE and stopped the active migratory behavior they formed stable focal adhesions marked by integrin and paxillin as well as actin.
source: However, once cells reach the RNE and stopped the active migratory behavior they formed stable focal adhesions marked by integrin and paxillin as well as actin (Videos 10 and 11, Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Videos 10 and 11, and Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Cells in the rim zone lacked basal enrichment of actin and paxillin, while cells in the invaginating region showed stable basal enrichment of Paxillin coinciding with the basal accumulation of actin.
source: While the cells in the rim zone lacked basal enrichment of actin and paxillin, cells in the invaginating region showed stable basal enrichment of Paxillin coinciding with the basal accumulation of actin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Video 12).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Video 12.

claim: The active migratory behavior observed for rim cells is confined to the zone that connects the developing RPE and the RNE, where cells move from one epithelial layer into the other by turning 180°.
source: This suggested that the active migratory behavior observed for rim cells is confined to the zone that connects the developing RPE and the RNE, where cells move from one epithelial layer into the other by turning 180°.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial distribution of migratory behavior.

claim: Once rim cells reach the inner layer of the cup they change to stable cell-ECM attachment and attain typical neuroepithelial morphology.
source: Once the cells reach the inner layer of the cup they change to stable cell-ECM attachment and attain typical neuroepithelial morphology.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in cell behavior and morphology.

claim: Knockdown of laminin resulted in impaired optic cup formation at 30 ss.
source: Knockdown of laminin resulted in impaired optic cup formation at 30 ss.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data showing the phenotype.

claim: Epithelial tissue accumulated at the temporal side of the optic cup in laminin morphants, giving the cup an S-shaped appearance instead of the C-shaped appearance seen in controls.
source: Epithelial tissue accumulated at the temporal side of the optic cup was observed, giving the cup an S-shaped appearance instead of the C-shaped appearance seen in controls (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Opo morphants recapitulated the S-shaped optic cup phenotype, although the severity of the phenotype was milder than in the laminin condition.
source: Indeed, opo morphants recapitulated the S-shaped optic cup phenotype, although the severity of the phenotype was milder than in the laminin condition (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Time-lapse imaging of laminin and opo morphants confirmed that the S-shaped phenotype was caused by impaired rim cell migration, as the speed of rim cells was reduced.
source: Time-lapse imaging of both conditions confirmed that the S-shaped phenotype was caused by impaired rim cell migration, as the speed of rim cells was reduced (Videos 13 and 14, Figure 4E,F,G).
evidence: This is supported by the time-lapse imaging data shown in Videos 13 and 14, and Figures 4E, 4F, and 4G.

claim: In the laminin morphant condition, overall tissue-wide apical marker distribution was not affected.
source: However, in the morphant condition used here we did not observe a strong effect on polarity. We only observed few ectopic apical domains within the neuroepithelium while overall tissue-wide apical marker distribution was not affected in the laminin morphants (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: No defects on apical marker distribution were observed in Opo morphants.
source: Similarly, no defects on apical marker distribution were observed in Opo morphants (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, Martinez-Morales et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B and citation to Martinez-Morales et al., 2009.

claim: Actomyosin accumulation was reduced in the invagination zone in both laminin and opo knockdown conditions.
source: Basally however, we noticed that actomyosin accumulation was reduced in the invagination zone in both laminin and opo knockdown conditions (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: Invagination angles were affected in laminin and opo knockdown conditions.
source: In addition, invagination angles were affected (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Both rim migration and actomyosin-assisted invagination were disturbed in laminin and opo knockdown conditions leading to the strong phenotypes observed.
source: This argued that both, rim migration and actomyosin-assisted invagination were disturbed in these conditions leading to the strong phenotypes observed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed defects in both processes.

claim: Interference with cell-ECM attachment leads to disturbance of the two cell behaviors involved in hemispheric RNE formation: rim cells cannot actively migrate due to impaired cell ECM-attachments and otherwise invaginating RNE cells failed to establish the basal actomyosin bias.
source: Together, these data imply that interference with cell-ECM attachment leads to disturbance of the two cell behaviors involved in hemispheric RNE formation, rim cells cannot actively migrate due to impaired cell ECM-attachments and otherwise invaginating RNE cells failed to establish the basal actomyosin bias.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data presented.

claim: In laminin morphants, rim cells localized Paxillin stably along the modified basement membrane instead of the dynamic foci seen in the control condition.
source: When we imaged the focal adhesion component Paxillin using mosaic Paxillin-mKate2 RNA injection, we observed that in laminin morphants the rim cells localized Paxillin stably along the modified basement membrane instead of the dynamic foci seen in the control condition (Video 15, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Video 15 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In opo morphants, Paxillin distribution was more transient than seen in the controls.
source: In opo morphants however, Paxillin distribution was more transient than seen in the controls (Video 16, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Video 16 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In both laminin and opo morphants, rim cells exhibited basal bleb-like protrusions instead of the lamellipodia observed in control embryos.
source: In both cases the rim cells exhibited basal bleb-like protrusions instead of the lamellipodia observed in control embryos (Videos 15 and 16, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Videos 15 and 16, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Basal blebs in morphant rim cells were extension of the plasma membrane, with short lived actin localization and devoid of myosin, showing the characteristic features of blebs.
source: These bleb-like protrusions were extension of the plasma membrane, with short lived actin localization and devoid of myosin, showing the characteristic features of blebs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Basal blebs were also observed when opo morphants cells were transplanted into control embryos, in line with a cell autonomous phenotype.
source: Such basal blebs were also observed when opo morphants cells were transplanted into control embryos, in line with a cell autonomous phenotype (Video 17, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, N = 4 out of 5 transplanted embryos).
evidence: This is supported by the transplantation experiment data shown in Video 17 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Morphant cells that failed to undergo active rim migration nevertheless reached the RNE, suggesting surrounding control cells most likely pull them along to their final positions.
source: The observation that morphant cells nevertheless reached the RNE underlines the collective characteristic of the migration as surrounding control cells most likely pull them along to their final positions (Video 17).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that morphant cells reach the RNE in transplantation experiments.

claim: Ezrin is a protein that links actin and the plasma membrane.
source: Ezrin is a protein that links actin and the plasma membrane and its knockdown has been shown to lead to increased blebbing and reduced migration rates of zebrafish prechordal plate precursor cells (Schepis et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schepis et al., 2012.

claim: Ezrin knockdown has been shown to lead to increased blebbing and reduced migration rates of zebrafish prechordal plate precursor cells.
source: Ezrin is a protein that links actin and the plasma membrane and its knockdown has been shown to lead to increased blebbing and reduced migration rates of zebrafish prechordal plate precursor cells (Schepis et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schepis et al., 2012.

claim: Ezrin knockdown did not affect the overall apicobasal polarity in the developing optic cup.
source: During RNE formation, we observed that ezrin knockdown did not affect the overall apicobasal polarity in the developing optic cup (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Ezrin knockdown specifically induced basal blebbing in the area where rim cells resided, whereas lateral sides of the rim cells and the pool of invaginating RNE cells were not affected.
